notes.meaning: God tells Moses to call his brother Aaron and Aaron's four sons out from among the people of Israel to serve as priests. A priest was a special minister chosen to represent the people before God and offer sacrifices. Moses did not keep this honor for himself or his own sons, but humbly obeyed the Lord by setting Aaron's family apart.

Moses is commanded to have holy clothing made for Aaron to give him dignity and beauty. These garments were called holy because they were set apart solely for sacred duties, not for everyday wear. Their rich appearance honored God's presence and pointed forward to the pure righteousness of Christ, our great High Priest.

God directs Moses to speak to the gifted craftsmen whom the Lord had blessed with special skill and wisdom. Aaron needed these garments for his consecration, which means being officially dedicated to God's holy service. Even practical and artistic talents come directly from God and can be used for His honor.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the phrase spirit of wisdom refers here to an artisan's natural intelligence and technical ability rather than a direct mention of the Holy Spirit.

notes.meaning: The craftsmen are given a list of six special garments to make: a chestpiece, an ephod, a robe, a woven tunic, a turban, and a sash. These garments were prepared for Aaron and his sons to equip them for their duties. Each piece helped show the reverence needed when entering the presence of the Lord.

The workers are told to gather gold, fine linen, and blue, purple, and scarlet yarns. These were the exact same costly materials used to make the tabernacle's sacred curtains. Wearing the same fabrics showed that the priest belonged completely to God's royal sanctuary.

The artisans must make the ephod out of finely spun linen woven with gold threads and rich colored yarns. The ephod was an ornate, sleeveless vest worn on the outside of the priest's longer robe. Its fine linen and gold thread displayed the purity and excellence required for standing before God.

The ephod had two shoulder straps attached at its top edges to connect the front piece to the back piece. These straps kept the vest secure around Aaron's body while he ministered. They also provided a firm base for the heavy gemstones that carried the names of the tribes.

The waistband of the ephod had to be woven in one continuous piece with the vest, using the same gold thread, colored yarns, and fine linen. Because it was woven into the fabric rather than stitched on later, it formed a single strong piece. This sash held the vest snugly in place during the priest's active service.

God commands Moses to take two onyx stones and carve the names of the twelve sons of Israel onto them. Six names went on one stone and the other six on the second stone, listed in the exact order of their birth. This order ensured that every tribe was remembered before God, from the oldest brother to the youngest.

A skilled jeweler was to carve the names deeply into the onyx stones, just like the mark made by an official signet seal. The stones were then mounted into frames of pure gold filigree. This careful craftsmanship showed that God's people are treasured and never forgotten.

Moses had to fasten both engraved stones onto the shoulder straps of the ephod as a memorial before the Lord. By wearing them, Aaron symbolically carried the whole nation of Israel on his shoulders into God's presence. In the same way, Jesus carries His people by His strength and continually intercedes for them.

The craftsmen were told to make gold settings and two chains of pure gold twisted like ropes. These braided chains attached the shoulder settings to the chestpiece below. They provided a strong, secure connection so the garments stayed together during worship.

The workers were to make a breastpiece of judgment with the same colorful yarns and gold thread as the ephod. It was called a breastpiece of judgment because the high priest wore it when seeking God's guidance and decisions for the nation. This reminded the priest to seek God's truth with fairness and devotion.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic translations refer to this item as the rational of judgment, drawing from Latin and Greek renderings for a sacred pouch used to receive divine decisions.

notes.meaning: The breastpiece was square when folded double, measuring about nine inches long and nine inches wide. Doubling the heavy woven cloth gave it enough strength to carry twelve gemstones without sagging. This fold also created an inner pouch that could hold sacred objects.

The first two rows of stones on the breastpiece held six distinct gems set firmly into the fabric. The top row had a ruby, a topaz, and an emerald, while the second row held a turquoise, a sapphire, and a diamond. Each stone sparkled with its own color, displaying the glorious variety among God's people.

The third row held a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst, and the fourth row held a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. All twelve stones were mounted in decorative gold filigree settings to hold them securely. This rich display showed that every single tribe held an honorable place before the Lord.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars caution that modern gem names do not reliably match the ancient Hebrew stone names, making exact identification uncertain.

notes.meaning: Each of the twelve stones was engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes of Israel. Aaron carried their names on his shoulders for strength, and he now wore them over his heart in love. This showed that God knows all His people individually and holds them dear to His heart.

Wires of pure gold were twisted like cords to make braided chains for the breastpiece. These chains fastened the top corners of the breastpiece directly to the ephod's shoulder pieces. They kept the list of Israel's tribes resting securely against the priest's chest.
